topic: Working with Sensors — Motion and Sound Sensors

slides.title: Session 20: Working with Sensors — Motion and Sound Sensors
bullets: THINK . CREATE . LEAD.
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students to Session 20 where we'll explore motion and sound sensors. Start with enthusiasm about how these sensors are all around us in India.
slides.graphics_description: ENpower logo with purple and gold colors. Background shows cartoon-style Indian students with diverse representation. Small icons of motion sensors and sound waves around the border.

slides.title: Sensors Are Everywhere Around Us!
bullets: Delhi Metro doors open automatically when you approach
Shopping mall lights turn on when you walk by
ISRO uses sensors to track spacecraft movement
Your phone detects when you speak to it
slides.speaker_notes: Connect to students' daily experiences. Ask them to think about automatic systems they've seen. These examples show motion and sound sensors working in Indian contexts.
slides.graphics_description: Split screen showing Delhi Metro automatic doors, mall corridor with motion-activated lights, ISRO mission control room, and a student speaking to a smartphone. All in colorful cartoon style.

slides.title: What Are Motion Sensors?
bullets: Motion Sensor: A device that detects movement of objects or people
PIR: Passive Infrared sensor that detects heat from moving objects
They sense when something moves in their range
Used as input devices to send signals to controllers
slides.speaker_notes: Define motion sensors clearly. Explain PIR in simple terms - it detects heat like our body heat. Emphasize that these are INPUT devices that collect information.
slides.graphics_description: Large cartoon motion sensor device in center. Arrows showing heat waves from a walking person being detected. Simple diagram showing sensor → controller → action flow.

slides.title: What Are Sound Sensors?
bullets: Sound Sensor: A device that detects sound waves and converts them to electrical signals
Microphone: A type of sound sensor that captures audio signals
They listen for sounds like clapping or speaking
Also input devices that send data to controllers
slides.speaker_notes: Connect sound sensors to familiar microphones. Explain how they convert sound waves into electrical signals that computers can understand. Reinforce the input device concept.
slides.graphics_description: Cartoon microphone with sound waves emanating from a student's mouth. Visual representation of sound waves being converted to electrical signals (zigzag lines).

slides.title: Human Motion and Sound Detector Challenge
bullets: Work in pairs to be human sensors
One person is the 'motion sensor' - detect movement
Other person is the 'sound sensor' - detect sounds
Practice triggering actions when you detect inputs
slides.speaker_notes: Students will role-play as sensors. Motion sensor student watches for movement and signals. Sound sensor student listens for specific sounds and signals. This helps them understand sensor-controller-actuator flow.
slides.graphics_description: Two cartoon Indian students working together. One has eyes wide open (motion sensor) watching another student move. Second student has hand to ear (sound sensor) listening. Action arrows between them.

slides.title: Input vs Output: Sensors vs Actuators
bullets: Sensors are INPUT devices - they collect information
Actuators are OUTPUT devices - they perform actions
Motion sensor (input) → Controller → Door opens (output)
Sound sensor (input) → Controller → Light turns on (output)
slides.speaker_notes: Clear distinction between input and output. Use concrete examples. Motion sensor detects (input), door motor opens door (output). Sound sensor hears clap (input), LED lights up (output).
slides.graphics_description: Flow diagram showing: Motion sensor → Controller box → Door opening. Below: Sound sensor → Controller box → Light bulb turning on. Use arrows and bright colors to show the flow.

slides.title: If-Then Logic with Sensors
bullets: IF motion is detected, THEN turn on the light
IF sound is heard, THEN open the door
IF no motion for 5 minutes, THEN turn off the fan
Controllers use this logic to make decisions
slides.speaker_notes: Introduce if-then logic as the brain of automation. Give clear examples. Ask students to create their own if-then statements. This prepares them for programming concepts later.
slides.graphics_description: Visual if-then flowchart with cartoon elements. Show decision diamond with 'Motion detected?' leading to 'YES → Light ON' and 'NO → Light OFF'. Use bright colors and simple shapes.

slides.title: Motion and Sound Sensors in India
bullets: Automatic hand sanitizer dispensers in hospitals
Voice-controlled elevators in Mumbai offices
Motion-activated street lights in smart cities
Sound-triggered emergency alarms in schools
slides.speaker_notes: Connect to Indian contexts students can relate to. Discuss how these technologies make life easier and safer. Ask students if they've seen these applications in their cities.
slides.graphics_description: Four panels showing: Hospital sanitizer dispenser, modern elevator with voice control, street lamp at night, school building with alarm system. All in Indian settings with diverse people.

slides.title: Indian Smart Systems Design Challenge
bullets: Design a smart system for an Indian school or home
Choose motion OR sound sensors as input
Write if-then logic for your system
Present your automation idea to the class
slides.speaker_notes: Students work in small groups to design practical automation systems. Encourage creativity while keeping solutions realistic. Focus on Indian contexts like monsoon-triggered window closers or festival sound-activated decorations.
slides.graphics_description: Students in groups around tables with paper and pencils, designing systems. Thought bubbles showing their ideas: smart classroom, automated home features. Indian school setting with diverse students collaborating.

slides.title: How Sensors Enable Automation
bullets: Automation: Technology that performs tasks automatically without human intervention
Sensors provide the 'eyes' and 'ears' for automated systems
Controllers process sensor data and make decisions
This creates smart, responsive environments
slides.speaker_notes: Define automation clearly. Help students understand that sensors are the starting point of all automated systems. They provide the information that allows systems to respond intelligently to their environment.
slides.graphics_description: Cartoon robot or smart home with sensor 'eyes' (motion sensors) and 'ears' (sound sensors). Arrows showing information flow to a central 'brain' (controller) that controls various outputs.

slides.title: Key Takeaways: Motion and Sound Sensors
bullets: Motion and sound sensors are input devices that detect environmental changes
PIR sensors detect heat, sound sensors convert sound waves to electrical signals
If-then logic helps controllers make decisions based on sensor data
These sensors enable automation in many Indian applications
slides.speaker_notes: Summarize the main learning points. Reinforce that sensors are inputs, they detect changes, and they enable automation through if-then logic. Connect back to the Indian examples discussed.
slides.graphics_description: Summary infographic with icons representing each key point: motion sensor icon, sound wave icon, if-then flowchart, and Indian flag with tech symbols. ENpower branding prominent.

slides.title: Next Steps: Keep Exploring!
bullets: Look for motion and sound sensors in your daily life
Think about new automation ideas for your home or school
Practice creating if-then logic statements
THINK . CREATE . LEAD with sensor technology!
slides.speaker_notes: Encourage continued exploration and observation. Students should start noticing sensors everywhere. This prepares them for future sessions on other sensor types and more complex automation projects.
slides.graphics_description: Inspiring image of diverse Indian students looking up with wonder, surrounded by floating icons of various sensors and smart devices. ENpower logo and tagline prominently displayed.
